title: Extension points, and when to add them

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, a new permitted type is added to a sealed interface, and the pattern-matching switches over it have no default branch. What follows?

options.text: Every switch that no longer covers all cases fails to compile
options.says: The page says every switch that is no longer exhaustive becomes a compile error.

options.text: Every switch hands the new type to its last case when it runs
options.says: The page says the compiler points at each switch that must be updated, before anything runs.

options.text: Every switch throws an exception once the new type reaches it
options.says: The page says the missing case is a compile error, so it is caught before the code runs.

questions.stem: Per this page, when is it the right time to introduce an interface as an extension point?

options.text: After a second or third concrete need for it has turned up
options.says: The page's Rule of Three: abstract after the second or third concrete need.

options.text: Before the first implementation, so every class starts open
options.says: The page calls creating interfaces before two implementations exist premature abstraction.

options.text: Once the code sits on a performance-critical tight loop path
options.says: The page lists performance-critical paths among the places OCP should not be applied.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: Premature abstraction is a pitfall: an extension point is introduced after the second or third concrete need, not before the first.
Adding a permitted type to a sealed interface makes every pattern-matching switch without a default that no longer covers it a compile error.
